Use the Real 2026 Rules

The actual CAT rules

questions per subject; minutes total.
Choose ELA or Math first. Respond before advancing; submitted Math and stand-alone ELA items cannot be revisited.

The legal review window

Return within the current ELA passage set, including passage-based revising/editing. After submitting that set, it is closed.

Which part of our old plan needs tightening?

The engine updates throughout the test. One early miss does not permanently close a score “ceiling.” How could obsessing over the first few items steal time from later evidence?

90 seconds = our training checkpoint, not an official limit

At the signal, check progress and remaining time. Make the best-supported response; do not replace thinking with a rapid-guessing sprint. This deck is a lesson, not a CAT scoring simulator.

How the review works11:00–12:00

Same Ladder, Sharper Diagnosis

Level 1 · Recognize

Name the object, unit, region, or relationship. One direct decision.

Level 2 · Connect

Translate the wording and carry out a short, familiar route.

Level 3 · Coordinate

Manage linked steps or competing interpretations without losing the target.

Level 4 · Transfer

Prove a boundary, diagnose a false method, or generalize a solution.

Every miss gets one primary tag.

C = careless/arithmetic · M = misread · G = content gap · T = timing · S = strategy. Explain the evidence for your tag aloud on at least three problems.
Level badges are instructional labels for this deck—not official DOE difficulty parameters. The PDFs’ “R” reading label maps to our “M” tag.

Minimum Overlap: Fill the Outside First

B 32Level 3
Of students, answer yes to and answer yes to . Every student answers both questions.
What is the least possible number who answer yes to both?

Try to avoid overlap

How many students are outside ? If you place into those seats first, what happens when those seats run out?

Make “least possible” earn its name

A lower bound is not enough. Describe an arrangement that achieves it. If every seat can be assigned consistently, the bound is attainable.

Transfer: Change One Count

B 2 / 32Level 4
A club has members. Of them, attend coding, attend robotics, and attend neither.
Find how many attend both. Then test the claim: “If neither rises by one while both class totals stay fixed, overlap must fall by one.”

The membership accounting model

Let and be class totals, both, neither, and everyone.
Every membership beyond one per person creates one double-count. Keep this identity balanced.

What stays invariant?

If only the neither count changes, which other region must compensate? Can quick before/after sketch disprove tempting verbal claim without recomputing everything?

Keep the Check, Cut the Rework

Structure before arithmetic

Overlap: region accounting.
Pizza: unordered pairs.
Spinners: ordered outcomes.
Intervals: objects versus gaps.

Target before submission

Difference: , not its reverse.
Inequality: count positive integers.
Expected value: total versus additional.
Arithmetic: preserve term structure.

Which single check would have saved the most points?

Pick one reviewed miss. Narrate the first decision you would now make, the likely wrong turn, and the brief check you will perform before advancing.

ELA repair · nonfiction passage34:00–36:00

Read the Whole Working Record

The Working Record

(1) At a school courtyard, two planting beds looked alike above ground. Beneath one, loose soil let water sink in; beneath the other, compacted soil shed water toward a drain.

(2) Students poured equal amounts of water onto the beds. They recorded drainage, checked that their measuring cups matched, and repeated the trial after switching cups.

(3) A gardener proposed loosening the second bed. The students kept the first bed unchanged as a comparison, treated the second, and tested both again.

(4) Their notebook included a trial with a leaking cup. Rather than erase it, they labeled the fault and repeated that measurement. A later student could then see why that trial was not used in the final comparison.

(5) The project’s final display showed observations, methods, and limitations. It invited visitors to judge how the claim had been tested rather than accept a polished result without its working record.

Read for movement of ideas

Read the entire passage first.
Write one short job label per paragraph: what changes from the beginning to the end?
Original transfer passage, not an excerpt from the PDFs. It targets the detail-to-purpose and whole-passage skills behind the Test B misses.
Skill basis: Test-B-English-Review.pdf · p.1; Set 2 Q2, Set 5 Q3, Set 1 Q6–Q7. Original lesson text.
ELA repair · purpose, not paraphrase36:00–38:00

From a Detail to Its Job

PurposeLevel 2
What job does the final sentence of paragraph perform?
Before answering, finish: “This detail shows ___, which supports the author’s point that ___.”
PurposeLevel 3
Why does the author include the leaking-cup trial in a passage about testing a claim?
Explain how paragraph connects the method in paragraph to the display in paragraph .

Use the deletion test

If paragraph vanished, what specific understanding would the reader lose? A detail’s subject is what it mentions; its job is what it does for the passage.
Detail → what it demonstrates → why the author needs it

ELA repair · summary and point of view38:00–40:00

Scope Is Part of Accuracy

SummaryLevel 3
Write one sentence that captures the whole passage. Your sentence must account for the starting problem, the testing process, and the final display—not just one memorable detail.
Point of viewLevel 4
How does the author’s selection of details reveal what the author values?
Support your interpretation with details from two different paragraphs; reject one competing interpretation.

Make every phrase pass the coverage test

Could your summary fit only paragraph ? If so, it is too narrow. Does your point-of-view claim rely on a stated prediction the passage never makes? If so, it goes too far.

True detail ≠ whole-passage summary.

A claim can be accurate locally and still fail the question’s scope. Compare your wording against the entire paragraph map.

ELA repair · fiction evidence window40:00–42:00

A Clash Between Belief and Evidence

In Search of the Unknown · Part A

(15) “Oh, you young fellows,” said the professor, smiling wearily, “you embark on a theory for destinations that don’t exist.”

(16) He leaned back in his chair, his amused eyes searching space for the imagery that made him smile.

(17) “Like swimming squirrels, you navigate with the help of Heaven and a stiff breeze, but you never land where you hope to—do you?”

(18) Rather red in the face, I said: “Don’t you believe the great auk to be extinct?”

(19) “Audubon saw the great auk.”

(20) “Who has seen a single specimen since?”

(21) “Nobody—except our correspondent here,” he replied, laughing.

Context and vocabulary

A narrator works under Professor Farrago. A correspondent claims to possess living great auks, birds generally believed extinct. The narrator rejects the claim.

Imagery: figurative comparison.
Audubon: a naturalist who studied birds.

Track whose mind you are reading

Mark the professor’s words separately from the narrator’s reaction. What does the comparison criticize: a lack of facts, a method of reasoning, or the narrator’s job performance? Hold the claim until Part B.
Test-B-English-Review.pdf · p.9, paragraphs 15–21. Robert W. Chambers, 1904; public-domain text verified via Project Gutenberg.
ELA repair · narrator and professional role42:00–44:00

What He Thinks Versus What He Does

In Search of the Unknown · Part B

(22) I laughed, too, considering the interview at an end, but the professor went on, coolly:

(23) “Whatever it is that our correspondent has—and I am daring to believe that it is the great auk itself—I want you to secure it for the society.”

(24) When my astonishment subsided my first conscious sentiment was one of pity. Clearly, Professor Farrago was on the verge of dotage—ah, what a loss to the world!

(25) I believe now that Professor Farrago perfectly interpreted my thoughts, but he betrayed neither resentment nor impatience. I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool’s errand was none of my conceiving.

Keep the viewpoints distinct

Dotage: perceived mental decline in old age.
Resentment: offended displeasure.

The narrator’s label is a character judgment, not an independent fact certified by the author.

Separate attitude from authority

What does the narrator think of the proposed expedition? What does he actually do? Can those answers differ without contradiction? Find the smallest span of text that proves each.

Make the Evidence Do the Work

B Set 3 Q4Level 3
In paragraphs , how do the professor’s remarks affect the narrator?
Make a precise claim about the reaction, then cite a word or action that supports it.
B Set 3 Q8Level 4
Which sentence in Parts A–B most clearly establishes the professional relationship between the men?
Quote only the needed words and explain why a nearby sentence shows attitude but not necessarily authority.

Use a claim–evidence–warrant chain

What does the question ask you to prove? Which exact sentence proves it? What is the logical bridge? Do not let a vivid insult substitute for evidence about the working relationship.

ELA repair · short original transfer items46:00–48:00

Editing: Plain, Exact, Complete

Sentence boundaryLevel 1
Revise this sentence without changing its meaning:
The students checked the cups, they repeated the trial.
TransitionLevel 2
Choose a transition and explain the relationship:
The first trial seemed conclusive. ___, the leaking cup made the result uncertain.
Formal styleLevel 3
Revise for precise, formal prose without exaggerating:
The team did a bunch of tests and totally proved that its fix was awesome.
Which words overstate the evidence? Which words need greater precision?

Explain the rule, not a preference

Can both sides of the comma stand alone? Does the transition signal the actual logic? Does “formal” mean longer—or more exact? Give the reason before you supply a revision.

ELA debrief · passage-set window48:00–50:00

Spend Time Where the Text Pays

Budget a set, not just each item

For a passage set: first read + questions + one review pass. Reading time is real work; do not label every passage’s first question a timing overrun.

Review with a stopping rule

Bookmark only uncertain items in the current set. On the final pass, change a choice only when you can name new textual or grammatical evidence.

Where does your ELA time leak?

Is it an overlong first read, repeated whole-passage rereading, or choosing between two options without identifying what the question asks? Which one change saves time without flattening comprehension?
Read fully → map the passage → answer with evidence → one legal check → submit

Final pacing plan · section allocation50:00–52:00

A Budget You Can Defend

A draft—not a measured optimum

+ +
minutes Math + minutes ELA + minutes flexible buffer. Choose section order using actual stamina and timing evidence.

The buffer is not a return ticket

Use it on the section still open. Once a section is submitted, extra time cannot buy a second look. No unused buffer can repair a locked Math response.

Defend the allocation

Would you start with your stronger Math section or protect ELA with fresh attention? Name one actual observation, not just a feeling, that supports your choice. What evidence would make you revise it?

Checkpoints Are a Compass, Not a Whip

Draft checkpoints for an 85-minute Math budget

On route—or repeating a strategy?Any time drift or target-reading slips?Submit only after the current check.
After itemSection elapsedCheck
17About 29 minutes

Use the number you can see

Translate section elapsed time into the overall countdown for your chosen order. How will you recognize a five-minute drift without checking the clock after every item?

Recover by changing the process

Cut repeated rereads and stalled routes first. At seconds, inspect progress; if stalled, make the strongest supported commitment. Preserve meaningful attempts—do not launch a blind sprint.
These are evenly spaced coaching checkpoints, not official section limits. ELA checkpoints belong at passage-set boundaries, not arbitrary item numbers.

Final pacing plan · spoken scripts54:00–56:00

Rehearse the Moment You Usually Drift

At the 90-second checkpoint

“What is asked? What have I ruled out? Am I making progress? I will use the strongest remaining evidence, commit, and advance.”

Two choices, little time

“I will name the exact difference between them, test it against the stem or text, and choose. I will not restart the entire problem.”

After a response that felt wrong

“That response is closed. One breath. New item, new evidence. I will not spend the next item’s attention on the last one.”

At a passage-set boundary

“I will check my marked items once, verify the evidence for any change, and submit. This set will then be closed.”

Rehearse—not just agree

Pick the script you are most likely to need. Say it at normal test speed. What physical action accompanies it: hand off the mouse, one breath, or eyes to the new stem?

Your Next Response Gets Full Attention

Teach back the route

Without looking: section order, time budgets, checkpoints, -second decision, passage-set review, and reset after a hard item.

One habit under pressure

Name your highest-leverage Math check and your highest-leverage ELA evidence move. Link each to one reviewed item.

Make it executable

If the first item feels harder than expected, what do you do? If you are five minutes behind at the checkpoint, what changes—and what does not? Say the plan once, clearly.
Leave with a decision process, not a prediction.
You have a route for reading the target, choosing a structure, checking evidence, and moving forward. Keep that route even when a single item feels uncomfortable.
